results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
**STEP 1. List of passages that answer the question**


---

**STEP 2. Answer**

You must keep records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return until the period of limitation for that return runs out. For most income‑tax returns that period is the number of years shown in the IRS tables (generally **3 years** unless a longer period applies such as 6 years for certain omissions). **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**  

For employment taxes you must keep all employment tax records for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later**. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**  

Records relating to property (assets) should be kept until the limitation period expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition—needed to determine depreciation, amortization, depletion, and basis. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**  

Keep copies of your filed tax returns at all times, as they help with future returns and amended returns. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**  

When records are no longer required for tax purposes, do not discard them until you confirm they need not be kept longer for other purposes such as insurance or creditor requirements. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**


**STEP 2 – Answer**

You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **To manage your business** – Record keeping lets you track income, expenses, assets and liabilities so you can make informed decisions and deal with banks or creditors effectively [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

2. **To prepare accurate tax returns** – Good records provide the evidence needed to support the income, deductions and credits you report. They also make it easier to prepare future returns and any amended ones [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

3. **To satisfy IRS requirements** – The IRS can inspect your records at any time. A complete set of records speeds up an examination and helps you explain reported items without dispute [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

4. **To separate business from personal activities** – Keeping a separate business checking account and recording transactions daily helps keep receipts, deposits and expenses distinct from personal funds, simplifying bookkeeping and tax compliance [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14).

5. **To comply with record‑retention periods** – You must retain records that support income or deductions until the statute of limitations runs out (generally three to six years, depending on the item). Employee‑tax records, asset documents, and other records must also be kept for specific periods [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

In short, keeping business records lets you run your business smoothly, file correct tax returns, and meet IRS and other regulatory requirements.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
**STEP 1 – Relevant passages**


---

**STEP 2 – Answer**

You decide which method to use when you file your first tax return that reports the business (for a sole‑prop, partnership, or S‑corp).

- **Cash method** – report income when received and expenses when paid.  
  “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it. You usually deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you pay them.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

- **Accrual method** – report income when earned, even if payment comes later, and expenses when incurred.  
  “Under an accrual method, you generally report income in the tax year you earn it, even though you may receive payment in a later year. You deduct or capitalize expenses in the tax year you incur them, whether or not you pay them that year.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

- **Inventory requirement** – If your business sells, manufactures, or otherwise accounts for inventory, you must use the accrual method for purchases and sales.  
  “If you must account for an inventory, you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for purchases and sales.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

- **Small‑business exception** – a small‑business taxpayer can elect to treat inventory as non‑incidental material or supplies and still use a cash method for all other items.  
  “Certain small‑business taxpayers can use the cash method of accounting and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

- **Combination method** – if you combine cash and accrual for different parts of the business, you must use the cash method for all income and expenses or the accrual method for both income and expenses; the combination can only be used if it “clearly shows your income and expenses and you use it consistently.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

**Bottom line**

- If you *do not* keep inventory (or meet the small‑business inventory exception), the **cash method** is the simplest and most common choice.  
- If you *do* keep inventory, you must use the **accrual method** for purchases and sales (or apply the small‑business exception if applicable).  

Choose the method when you file your first return that includes Schedule C (Form 1040) or the appropriate business form, and use the same method consistently for both income calculation and bookkeeping.

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
**STEP 1**  


**STEP 2**  

To check your workplace for hazards, start with a routine **self‑inspection** (1).  Knowledgeable and experienced workers should conduct these inspections themselves in order to see if potential hazards exist and whether they are under control [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).  Use the handbook’s **self‑inspection checklists** as a starting point; the checklists are tailored to general industry work sites and help you identify, control, and monitor hazards [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).  

When you complete a checklist, **compile the findings** with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and equipment logs (e.g., maintenance logs, incident reports).  Combine this data to determine where challenges exist and then refer to OSHA standards and other resources for solutions [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).  

Take note of the checklist format that can be adapted to your business: each inspection should record the worksite name, inspected area, inspector, date, and whether safety and health programs, reporting procedures, hazard control, and worker participation are in place [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9).  

For a more thorough assessment, you can request a **no‑cost, confidential visit** from OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program.  Highly trained consultants can identify safety and health hazards and recommend how to fix them, advise on compliance, train workers, and help build or improve your safety program.  They can focus on a single concern or conduct a comprehensive hazard assessment of the entire facility [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).  

In summary, examine your workplace regularly with structured self‑inspections, use the handbook’s checklists and record‑keeping guidance, and optionally enlist an OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program consultant for a deeper hazard review.

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
**STEP 1.**  


**STEP 2.**  
Yes. The IRS allows a sole proprietor to deduct the ordinary and necessary expenses incurred while traveling away from home for business purposes. Those deductions include:

* **Transportation costs** – you may deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and a temporary business destination. Fares for taxis, commuter buses, and limousines between an airport or station and your hotel (or between the hotel and your work location) are also deductible. You may use either actual expenses or the standard mileage rate (or a rental‑car business‑use portion) for vehicle travel [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
* **Meals** – you can deduct the cost of meals while on a business trip, but the deduction is generally limited to 50 % of the expense [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  
* **Lodging** – stay‑overnight accommodations are fully deductible when the trip is overnight or long enough that you need sleep or rest to perform your duties [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).  
* **Other incidental expenses** – such as baggage, shipping of business items, dry cleaning, telephone calls, and tips are deductible [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41).

To qualify, the travel must be **ordinary and necessary** for your business, and you must be away from your regular place of business for longer than an ordinary day’s work [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
**STEP 1. List of passages that answer the question**  


---

**STEP 2. Answer**

An executive summary is a brief section of the business plan that gives the reader a quick overview of what you want to accomplish.  According to the SBA Business Planning Guide, it should typically be one or two paragraphs and include:

- A description of the business idea (what the business does) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
- The amount of money you need and how you plan to use it (money required, purpose of the funds) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
- The amount of money you will contribute or have already invested in the venture (equity invested) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  
- A brief schedule of your goals or milestones (timeline for reaching key objectives) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).  

The executive summary should be written last, after the rest of the plan is complete, so that it can accurately reflect the full details of the business. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).



**Sources:**

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
**STEP 1.**  USING: [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

Describe your target market by first defining the niche that your business serves – the group of customers who will benefit most from what you offer. Identify those customers and describe their characteristics such as age, gender, income, lifestyle, or industry, geographic region or usage patterns. Tailor the description to the type of market you are addressing: for consumer (household) markets, segment by demographics, geographic location, economic status, lifestyle, or benefits sought; for business markets, segment by industry, company size, location or application of the product/service [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14).  

After painting the picture of the ideal customer, estimate the overall size and growth potential of the target segment. Use population data, industry reports, sales‑tax statistics, or other credible sources to quantify how large the market is and how fast it is expanding. Then estimate the percentage of that total market you anticipate capturing, grounding the figure in realistic assumptions [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14).  

Include the target‑market description in the marketing portion of your business plan, where you also outline competition, entry strategy, location considerations, industry trends, distribution, promotion, and pricing [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6),  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7),  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8),  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10),  
[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)

These passages state that a shop that serves the public is a public accommodation covered by the ADA, that barrier removal must be “readily achievable,” and give concrete examples of required accessibility features (accessible entrance, door hardware, parking, etc.).

---

**STEP 2 – Answer**

Yes.  
If you own, operate or lease a shop that provides goods or services to the public, you are a “public accommodation” under the ADA. The statute requires you to remove physical barriers that are **readily achievable**, meaning barriers that can be removed without undue expense or difficulty given the size and resources of your business [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  

Typical required features include:  

* **An accessible entrance** – at least one entrance must be free of steps or have a ramp, lift, or other low‑rise entry that is not more than a 1:12 slope. Where an accessible entrance is not possible, a second entrance or alternate service (e.g., delivery) can be provided if that is readily achievable [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  
* **Door hardware** – a door that is at least 36 in. wide, with lever or push‑type handles that do not require a tight grasp [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).  
* **Accessible parking** – at least one accessible parking space with a 36‑in. wide access aisle and a clear vertical clearance of 98 in. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  
* **Internal accessibility** – clear aisles of at least 36 in. wide, accessible routes to shelves and counters, and at least 30 in. by 48 in. clearance in front of each accessible counter (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 10, page 12).  

If you cannot make any of these features readily achievable, the ADA allows you to provide an alternative service (e.g., home delivery, an accessible service counter elsewhere, or assistance from staff) that is itself readily achievable (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 10, page 16).  

In short, you are required to make your shop reasonably wheelchair accessible, but the law recognises that some adjustments may need to be phased in as resources allow.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
**STEP 1. List of passages that address the exemption question**


**STEP 2. Answer**

You are exempt from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness record‑keeping requirements only if one of the following applies [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14):

1. Your establishment had **10 or fewer workers during the entire last calendar year** (see 29 CFR 1904.1).  
2. Your business is in a **low‑hazard industry** listed in 29 CFR Part 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A.

If you do not meet either of those conditions, you must maintain OSHA Form 300 and Form 301 logs for all recordable injuries and illnesses and keep them on the worksite for at least five years [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14).

results.question: how long do i keep injury records
results.answer:
**STEP 1.**  


**STEP 2.**

### Do I need an EIN?

You must obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) if you:
* pay wages to one or more employees, or
* file certain pension or excise tax returns (​irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 6).  
If you have no employees and no special filings, you may use your Social‑Security number instead, but you can also choose to obtain an EIN for business purposes (​irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 4).

### What accounting method goes with an EIN?

The recording method you use for income and expenses is **not** determined by whether you have an EIN.  
When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (or another form appropriate to your entity), you must choose a method and keep it consistently:

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**


**STEP 2 – Answer**

Choose an accounting method that fits the nature of your business:

* **Cash method** – Report income when you receive it and deduct expenses when you pay them. Most sole‑proprietors and small businesses that do **not** keep an inventory use this method because it is simpler and the IRS allows it normally.  
* **Accrual method** – Report income when you earn it (the “all‑events” test is met) and deduct or capitalise expenses when they are incurred, whether or not they are paid. If your business **maintains inventories** of merchandise, raw materials, work in process, or finished goods, you must generally use the accrual method to account for purchases and sales (or treat inventories as non‑incidental materials if you qualify as a small business) (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5;[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16).  

If you select a method, you must **use the same method** to both figure taxable income and keep your books, and the method must clearly show your income (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5; irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 14).  

A **combination method** (cash for some items, accrual for others) is allowed only if it still clearly reflects income and is used consistently; for example, the IRS permits an accrual method for inventory while using cash for all other items, but you must treat the whole as a cash method if the cash element is used (irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 14‑16).

In short, use **cash** if you have no inventory or are a small business exempt from inventory accruals; use **accrual** if you maintain inventory or must match income with expenses in the same year. If you need to mix methods, follow the IRS rules on combination methods and seek IRS approval if later you wish to change [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that directly explain the difference**


**STEP 2 – Answer**

Cash and accrual accounting differ only in the timing of when income and expenses are reported.

* **Cash method** – Income is included only in the tax year in which it is actually received, and expenses are deducted (or capitalised) in the year in which they are actually paid. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

* **Accrual method** – Income is included in the tax year in which it is earned, even if payment is received later, and expenses are deducted (or capitalised) in the year in which they are incurred, regardless of when payment is made. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

The two publications also illustrate this timing difference: an accrual‐method taxpayer who buys office supplies in December 2025 can deduct that expense in 2025 because the liability was fixed and the goods were received that year, even though payment may occur in January 2026. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

In contrast, a cash‑method taxpayer would only claim the deduction when the payment is actually made. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  

Thus, the key distinction is whether transactions are recorded when cash changes hands (cash method) or when the economic events of earning or incurring happen (accrual method).

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
**Answer**

Yes.  A small business is required to provide at least one wheelchair‑accessible entrance (or an accessible route to the entry), and it must give customers who use wheelchairs a path to the area where goods or services are offered.  The ADA Guide for Small Business says:

* “Providing physical access to a facility from public sidewalks, public transportation, or parking is…basic to making goods and services available to people with disabilities.”  
* “When a business has two public entrances, in most cases, only one must be accessible.”

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**Step‑by‑step guide to starting a business and keeping your taxes organized**

**1. Decide on a legal structure**  
- A new owner must choose a business form (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation or LLC).  This decision determines the tax‑return forms you’ll file and the record‑keeping you’ll need.  
  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=2)

**2. Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN)**  
- You need an EIN if you will pay employees, file pension or excise tax returns, or want to use an EIN in place of your SSN for the business.  
- Apply online at IRS.gov/EIN, by phone, or by mailing Form SS‑4.  
  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  *(page 4 in the 583 publication also covers this)*

**3. Pick a fiscal year**  
- If you file your first return with a calendar year (Jan 1 – Dec 31), you can keep using it unless you get IRS approval to change it.  
- A fiscal year is a 12‑month period ending on the last day of any month other than December.  
- Change a tax year by filing Form 1128; fees may apply.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  *(also see page 6 for change instructions)*

**4. Choose an accounting method**  
- **Cash method**: income is reported when received and expenses when paid.  
- **Accrual method**: income is reported when earned, expenses when incurred.  
- Certain businesses (e.g., with inventory) are required to use accrual.  
- You choose the method on your first income‑tax return (Schedule C).  
  

**5. Set up bookkeeping**  
- **Single‑entry**: simplest; tracks a daily cash summary and monthly totals.  
- **Double‑entry**: records debits and credits in journals and ledgers, providing checks and balances.  
- Many small businesses start with single‑entry and move to double‑entry as they grow.  
  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

**6. Keep required records**  
- Maintain records that support every item of income or deduction on a return until the applicable period of limitations ends (usually 3‑6 years for tax returns, 4 years for employment taxes).  
- Keep copies of filed returns for future reference.  
- Preserve asset‑related records until the period of limitations expires after a disposition.  
  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

**7. Use the proper forms for payments to others**  
- For employees, collect SSNs (Form W‑4) and provide them with Form W‑2.  
- For non‑employees who receive ≥ $600 in a year, obtain a taxpayer ID (SSN or EIN) on Form W‑9 and file Form 1099‑MISC or 1099‑NEC.  
- If a payee fails to provide an ID, you may need to apply backup withholding.  
  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)

**8. File your taxes on time**  
- File Form 1040 with Schedule C for sole proprietors, and additional forms (e.g., 941, 940, 1099 family) as required.  
- Pay any tax due by the due date of the return (e.g., April 15 for calendar‑year 2025) to avoid penalties and interest.  
  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)

**9. Use available tools and assistance**  
- The Small Business Administration (SBA) and Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) offer counseling, training, and resources for record‑keeping and tax matters.  
  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=53)

---

**In short:**  
1. Pick a business form → 2. Get an EIN → 3. Choose a tax year → 4. Select a cash or accrual method → 5. Set up single‑ or double‑entry bookkeeping → 6. Preserve records for the required period → 7. Obtain IDs and file information returns for payments → 8. File and pay taxes on time → 9. Leverage SBA/SBDC help.  

These steps, drawn directly from the IRS and SBA publications, give you a clear path to launching your business while keeping your taxes organized.

**Answer**

To keep employees safe and your premises accessible you should:  

1. **Carry out routine self‑inspections.** Use the OSHA‑approved checklists to identify hazards, control them, and verify that controls remain effective.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)  

2. **Understand and meet OSHA standards and the General Duty Clause.**  Review the applicable OSHA regulations (e.g., 29 CFR 1910, 1926, 1928, 1930) and make sure your workplace is free from recognized hazards likely to cause death or serious harm.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

3. **Maintain safe exit routes, doors, and emergency plans.**  Ensure all required exits are unobstructed, doors open from the exit side, and that signs, lighting and handrails meet OSHA requirements.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=12)  

4. **Provide worker training.**  Offer OSHA‑approved training for hazards specific to your operations and for general safety practices, and consider OSHA Outreach Training for basic workplace safety.  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=12)  

5. **Use OSHA On‑Site Consultation.**  Request a free, confidential visit from an OSHA consultant to identify hazards, explain compliance requirements, and help improve your safety program.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

6. **Remove “readily achievable” barriers under the ADA.**  If you serve the public, you must eliminate physical barriers—e.g., steps at entrances, narrow aisles, non‑graspable door hardware—unless removal is not “readily achievable.”  [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

7. **Make entrances accessible.**  Install ramps no steeper than a 1:12 slope, provide handrails for slopes above 1:20, and add accessible loops or lifts where steps cannot be removed.  Sign all new or alternative accessible entrances.  [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

8. **Provide accessible parking and routes.**  Offer designated accessible parking spaces with an access aisle at least 8 ft wide (van‑accessible spaces wider), mark the spaces with the international accessibility symbol, and ensure a level, slip‑resistant route to the accessible entrance.  [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)  

9. **Make sales and service counters accessible.**  Keep counter tops at or below 36 in. above the floor and provide a clear 30 × 48 in. space in front for wheelchairs, or add an auxiliary counter.  [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  

10. **Prioritize barrier removal.**  Start with access from sidewalks, parking, and public transit; then clear the path to service areas, public restrooms, and finally other interior barriers.    

By following these OSHA‑ and ADA‑based steps you will protect workers from workplace hazards, meet federal safety requirements, and ensure that your premises remain accessible to all customers and visitors.

runs.question: how long do i keep tax records
runs.answer:
**USING:** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15)

---

**Answer**

You must keep your tax records **at least as long as the statute of limitations for the relevant tax matter** (or longer if other obligations require it):

- For most income‑tax returns, the period of limitations is **3 years** (**IRS Publication 583, p. 15, Table 3**).  
- If you omit income that is more than 25 % of the amount reported, the limitation extends to **6 years** (**IRS Publication 583, p. 15, Table 3**).  
- A fraudulent return is **not limited** (**IRS Publication 583, p. 15, Table 3**).

- **Employment‑tax records** must be kept for **at least 4 years after the date the tax becomes due or is paid** (whichever is later) (**IRS Publication 583, p. 16**).

- **Records relating to property** (assets) must be kept until the period of limitations expires for the year in which the property is disposed of in a taxable disposition (**IRS Publication 583, p. 16**).

- Copies of your **filed tax returns** should be retained because they help prepare future returns and may be needed if you file an amended return (**IRS Publication 583, p. 16**).

- If your records are no longer needed for tax purposes, do **not discard them until you verify that no other parties (e.g., insurers, creditors) require a longer retention period** (**IRS Publication 583, p. 16**).

runs.question: why do i need to keep business records
runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that support an answer**

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11),

[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)

**STEP 2 – Answer**

You need to keep business records for several practical and legal reasons:

1. **Financial management and access to credit** – Business income‑statement and balance‑sheet records help you deal with banks or creditors and manage the day‑to‑day business [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

2. **Separating business from non‑business receipts** – Records identify the source of receipts so you can distinguish taxable business income from non‑taxable or personal income [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

3. **Tracking deductible expenses** – If you forget an expense until you prepare a tax return, the deduction may be lost; timely record‑keeping ensures you deduct all allowable costs [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

4. **Preparing and supporting tax returns** – The tax return must be backed by records that support the income, deductions, and credits reported; a complete set of records speeds up an IRS examination (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 11; irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 12).

5. **Compliance with statutory retention requirements** – Records are required to be maintained for the period of limitations on income‑tax returns, for employment‑tax records (at least 4 years after the tax becomes due or is paid), and for assets until the period of limitations on the year the property is disposed of [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

6. **Evidence for audits and legal needs** – When the IRS or other agencies examine the business, your records provide evidence of your financial activity and help you defend or clarify reported items [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

7. **Occupational safety and health compliance** – OSHA requires that injury and illness records be kept at the worksite for at least five years, and certain fatal or serious injury reports must be submitted within specific deadlines; failure to keep these records can result in penalties [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).

These reasons collectively explain why keeping thorough, accurate business records is essential for financial control, tax compliance, legal defensibility, and occupational‑safety reporting.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**STEP 1**  


---

**STEP 2**  

When you file your first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for your business, you must select an accounting method.  
You may choose either the **cash method** or the **accrual method** (or a special or combination method if the IRS allows it) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

**Cash method** – you report income in the year you receive it and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
**Accrual method** – you report income in the year you earn it (even if payment comes later) and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred, whether or not you pay them that year [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

Whether you can use the cash method depends on whether you have inventory to account for.  
If you sell goods, use raw materials or keep any inventory, the IRS generally requires the accrual method for purchases and sales unless you qualify as a *small‑business taxpayer* (IRS Publication 334, page 16).  
Most sole proprietors who have no inventory find the cash method easier to maintain [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  

Thus, pick the method that matches your business activity:  
- **No inventory** → Cash method is usually appropriate.  
- **Inventory required** → Accrual method is generally required (unless you qualify for a small‑business exception).  

If you need to change from one method to another later, you must obtain IRS approval, generally by filing Form 3115 (IRS Publication 334, page 16).

These three sections give the specific steps and tools an employer can use to check for workplace hazards.

---

**STEP 2 – How to check your workplace for hazards**

1. **Conduct routine workplace self‑inspections**.  
   An effective way to identify workplace hazards is for knowledgeable and experienced workers to conduct routine safety and health inspections (i.e., self‑inspections). The only way to know if potential hazards exist and if they are under control is to assess work processes directly [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

2. **Use OSHA‑provided self‑inspection checklists**.  
   Checklists in the handbook are intended for general industry workplaces and can be a starting point for identifying hazards. They give you an indication of where to begin taking action to make your business safer and more healthful for your workers [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).  

3. **Complete a safety‑program inspection form**.  
   The handbook includes a form that prompts you to verify the presence of key elements—such as a safety and health program, worker training, and active workplace inspections—and notes whether each element is in place .  
   The form also asks whether workers are trained to identify and control hazards and whether they are involved in inspections, which helps ensure that hazards are identified and managed effectively [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9).

4. **Compile and analyze the data**.  
   Compile information from your completed checklists with workplace injury and illness records, worker training information, and process and equipment information (e.g., maintenance logs, failure‑incident reports). Use this data to pinpoint where hazards exist and to track the effectiveness of controls [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8).

5. **Seek a no‑cost, confidential On‑Site Consultation visit** (optional but recommended).  
   OSHA’s On‑Site Consultation Program offers highly trained safety professionals who can help you identify hazards, advise on compliance, train workers, and improve your safety program. A visit can focus on a single concern or a thorough hazard assessment of the entire facility [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90).  

By following these steps—regular self‑inspections, using checklists, employing the inspection form, compiling comprehensive data, and, if needed, inviting a consultation—you can systematically check your workplace for hazards and keep them under control.

runs.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
runs.answer:
**STEP 1**  


---

**STEP 2**  

Cash method versus accrual method are two primary ways the IRS allows a business to report its income and expenses.

- **Cash method**:  
  *You report income in the tax year you receive the cash, and you normally deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you actually pay them.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
  *Under the cash method, you generally deduct expenses in the tax year in which you actually pay them.* [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)

- **Accrual method**:  
  *You generally report income in the tax year you earn it, even though you may receive payment in a later year, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you incur them, whether you pay them that year or not.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
  *Under an accrual method of accounting, you generally report income in the year earned and deduct or capitalize expenses in the year incurred.* [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

The key distinction, therefore, is the timing of recognition: cash accounting records transactions when money actually changes hands, while accrual accounting records transactions when they are earned or incurred, aligning income with the related expenses in the same period.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
**USING:** [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34), [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40), [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

---

### Yes – you can deduct ordinary and necessary business‑travel expenses, subject to the rules below.

1. **Travel must be “away from home.”**  
   • The IRS requires that the trip be away from the general area of your tax home **for a period substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work** and that you need to rest or sleep to meet the demands of your work while away from home. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

2. **Deductible transportation costs**  
   • You may deduct the cost of travel by airplane, train, bus, or car between your home and your business destination.  
   • Fares for taxis, commuter buses, or limousines between an airport or station and your hotel, or between the hotel and your work location away from home, are also deductible. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
   • Baggage and shipping of T‑shirts, samples, or display material between your regular and temporary work locations are deductible. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)  
   • If you use your own vehicle, you may deduct real operating costs (actual expenses) or the standard mileage rate (70¢ per mile for 2025) for traveling away from home on business, and you may also deduct business‑related tolls and parking fees. (irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 40; page 34)

3. **Meals and lodging**  
   • If the trip is overnight (or long enough to require a place to sleep), you can deduct the cost of meals and lodging. You may use either actual expenses or the IRS standard‑meal allowance, but in most cases only **50 % of meal expenses** are deductible. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
   • Lodging costs are deductible in full, provided the stay is business‑related. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)

4. **Other related deductions**  
   • Cleaning (dry cleaning and laundry) done while on the trip, business telephone calls, fax costs, and tips paid for transportation or lodging are deductible. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)  
   • If you rent a car on the trip, you can deduct only the portion of the rental that is used for business. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)

5. **Local business transportation**  
   • While local transportation between work sites within your tax‑home area is *not* deducted as travel expenses, it is deductible under the car‑and‑truck expense rules. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=34)

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
**Step 1 – Passages that support an answer**

- [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  
- [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7)  
- [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8)  
- [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  
- [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Step 2 – Answer**

Yes.  Under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) a private business that serves the public is a **public accommodation** and is required to remove “barriers that are readily achievable” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  The ADA specifically applies to existing facilities; they are not exempt by a “grandfather” provision [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).

*What must be made accessible?*  
- **Entrances**: Every business must provide at least one accessible entrance from public sidewalks, parking, or public transportation.  An accessible entrance requires a ramp with a maximum slope of 1:12, a clear width of at least 36 inches, handrails where the slope is greater than 1:20 or the vertical rise exceeds 6 inches, and a wide landing if the entrance is not on a level approach [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- **Interior circulation**: A continuous accessible route must be provided from the entrance to all places where goods and services are offered.  A minimum 36‑inch wide aisle is required, with larger turning spaces (60 inches for a 180° turn) where necessary [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14).  
- **Doors**: Doors to the public space must have a clear width of at least 36 inches when fully open.  If a door is narrower, the opening can be enlarged or a “swing‑clear” hinge used; inaccessible handles must be replaced or modified [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12).  
- **Counters and service points**: A lowered section of each sales or service counter that is no higher than 36 inches and at least 36 inches long must be made available [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  
- **Parking**: Accessible parking spaces must be provided, along with an access aisle at least 5 ft. wide for cars (or 8 ft. for vans) and an accessible route to the entrance that has no steps or steep slopes [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8).  

If creating such facilities is not “readily achievable,” the ADA allows a shop to provide alternative services (e.g., staff assistance, home‑delivery) that enable customers with disabilities to access goods or services (ada_guide_small_business.pdf, page 7, page 11).  

In short, **you are required to remove barriers that can be readily achieved; otherwise you must offer an alternative means of access**.  The documents do not impose a single deadline, but the requirement is ongoing and tied to the business’s ability to act practicably.

runs.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**


**STEP 2 – Answer (using only the cited passages)**  

You are exempt from OSHA injury‑and‑illness recordkeeping only if **both** of the following conditions apply:

1. During every calendar year of the previous year you had **10 or fewer workers**  
  (29 CFR 1904.1) – (osh…handbook.pdf, page 14).  
2. Or, you operate in one of the **low‑hazard industries** listed in 29 CFR 1904, Subpart B, Appendix A – (osh…handbook.pdf, page 14).

If you do not meet either condition, you must **record every occupational injury or illness that requires more than first aid on OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses)**, and you must keep a detailed Form 301 for each recordable case (osh…handbook.pdf, page 14).  

In addition, **all employers**—regardless of size or industry—must **report** the following to OSHA within the specified timeframes:  
* Fatalities: within 8 hours (osh…handbook.pdf, page 14)  
* In‑patient hospitalizations, amputations, and loss of an eye: within 24 hours (osh…handbook.pdf, page 14).

If your establishment employs **100 or more workers in a designated high‑hazard industry**, you must also **electronically submit** the contents of Forms 300 and 301 annually by March 2 of the following year (osh…handbook.pdf, page 15).  

Therefore, whether you are exempt depends on your worker count and industry classification as described above. If you have more than 10 employees or work in a high‑hazard sector, you are **not exempt** from injury recordkeeping.

runs.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5),  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15),  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4),  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12),  
[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13),  
[[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  

---

**STEP 2 – Answer**

**Writing a Business Plan**

1. **Start with a clear outline** – the SBA guide says the first step is to organize “your effort to gather and evaluate information about your business” and that a business plan should contain a cover page, table of contents, executive summary, business description, management plan, market analysis, and money (financial) section [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

2. **Cover page** – includes company name, address, phone, owners’ contact info, and date [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

3. **Table of contents** – optional, but helps readers navigate [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

4. **Executive summary** – a brief paragraph that presents the idea, funding needed, and a high‑level schedule of goals [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4).

5. **Business section** – describe the industry, product or service, competitive advantage, facilities, equipment, regulatory requirements, and future projections [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12).

6. **Management section** – identify the legal form of the business, ownership percentages, key people’s roles, qualifications, and advisers; include resumes and legal documents in exhibits [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13).

7. **Marketing section** – explain the target market, competition, distribution, promotion, and pricing (sba_business_planning_guide.pdf, page 14–15).  

8. **Money section** – include historical statements (if any), three‑year income projections, cash‑flow projections, balance sheet, and break‑even analysis; also show a sources‑and‑uses schedule and equity invested [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).

**Setting Up Accounting**

1. **Choose an accounting method** – The IRS says you choose either **cash** or **accrual** when you file your first tax return, and you may later change it only with IRS approval [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
   *Cash method*: report income when received and deduct expenses when paid.  
   *Accrual method*: report income when earned and deduct expenses when incurred.

2. **Bookkeeping system** – Decide between a **single‑entry** system, which records income and expenses in a simple cash‑flow format, or a **double‑entry** system, which uses journals and ledgers for debits and credits and provides built‑in checks [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).  
   • Double‑entry gives more control and is suitable if you expect to track assets, liabilities, and equity.  
   • Single‑entry may suffice for very small, cash‑only operations.

3. **Maintain books and records** – For either system you must keep detailed, machine‑sensible records that can be reconciled with your tax return; they must include a chart of accounts, control procedures, and sufficient detail to verify all entries [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=15).

4. **Later changes** – If you later need to change your accounting method or the treatment of a material item, you must file Form 3115 and may need to pay a user fee [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=17).

These steps, taken together, give you a complete business plan ready for investors or lenders and a solid accounting foundation that meets IRS requirements.

runs.question: what should i track for taxes and for travel expenses
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.  Passages that directly answer the question**


**STEP 2.  Answer**

To keep your books in order and to satisfy the IRS you should track the following for **tax purposes**:

1. **Gross receipts and sales** – record every sale, and make sure to include any state and local sales taxes that you collect from customers, but do **not** include those sales‑tax amounts in your business income (IRS‑334, page 31).  
2. **Inventory** – record beginning and ending balances, as well as any purchases or withdrawals for personal use, so you can accurately calculate cost of goods sold (IRS‑334, page 31).  
3. **Excise taxes** – keep a separate record of any excise taxes you pay on manufacturing, fuel, or vehicle use. These taxes are reported on Form 720, Form 2290, etc., and should be tracked for compliance (IRS‑583, page 8).  
4. **Business mileage** – if you drive for work, track all business miles. You must choose either the standard mileage rate (70 ¢/mile for 2025) or actual expenses and keep a mileage log (IRS‑334, page 35).  
5. **Actual car expenses** – if you elect actual expense deduction, track depreciation, lease or loan payments, registration, tolls, parking, insurance, and fuel (IRS‑583, page 15).  

For **travel expenses** you should record and keep receipts for the following categories so you can claim the deductions on Schedule C (or an accounting statement):

1. **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, or car between home and the travel destination (IRS‑334, page 40).  
2. **Taxi, commuter bus, limousine** – fares for airport or hotel to work sites (IRS‑334, page 40).  
3. **Baggage and shipping** – costs for sending baggage, samples, or display materials between locations (IRS‑334, page 40).  
4. **Car or truck** – if you use your own vehicle on a trip, record either the standard mileage rate or the actual expenses plus business‑related tolls and parking (IRS‑334, page 35 & page 40).  
5. **Meals and lodging** – keep receipts for meals (subject to a 50 % limitation) and lodging when the trip is overnight or long‑enough that rest is required (IRS‑334, page 40).  
6. **Other incidental expenses** – cleaning, telephone calls (including fax or other communication), and tips related to the travel (IRS‑334, page 41).  

By maintaining these records—sales receipts, inventory logs, excise‑tax statements, mileage logs, and travel receipts—you’ll be able to calculate accurate income, deduct allowable expenses, and comply with IRS reporting requirements.

### Do I need an EIN?

- If you pay wages to one or more employees or file pension or excise‑tax returns, you **must have an EIN** [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  
- Sole proprietors, LLCs, corporations, and partnerships receive an EIN for tax‑filing and reporting purposes, but a sole proprietor with **no employees** may use his or her Social Security number or may choose to obtain an EIN instead of the SSN for business identification [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=4).

### What accounting method comes with an EIN?

- The IRS does **not attach a specific accounting method to an EIN**; you choose the method when you file your first tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040) for the business [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
- You may use either the **cash method** (income and expenses are reported in the year they are received or paid) or the **accrual method** (income is reported when earned, expenses when incurred).  
- If you have inventory, the accrual method is generally required unless you qualify as a small‑business taxpayer who can treat inventories as non‑incidental material or supplies [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).

In short, having an EIN does **not determine** your accounting method; you select a method (cash, accrual, or a combination) that best fits your business’s financial activities.

runs.answer:
**STEP 1 – Passages that answer the question**

---

**STEP 2 – Answer**  

For small businesses, the most common and tax‑favorable way to provide health coverage to employees is to purchase a **group‑hospitalization and medical insurance plan** that qualifies for the federal tax treatment described in the IRS Publication 334.

* The plan must be a **qualified health‑insurance plan** that you offer to **eligible employees** (the plan is typically sold to the employer and then paid for by the employer, with employees paying a share if they choose).  
* Premiums that you pay for that coverage are **fully deductible** as a business expense (see “Insurance” and “Fringe benefits” on page 37) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=37).  
* If the plan meets the requirements for the **small‑employer health‑insurance premium credit**, you may be able to receive a refundable credit equal to a percentage of the premiums you pay for employees (Form 8941) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=20).  

Typical choices that meet these criteria are fully‑integrated **HMO, PPO, or high‑deductible plans** sold through the employer‑only marketplace, or a **self‑funded” or “SIMPLE” group plan. The key points are:

1. **Group coverage** – the plan must be offered to a group of employees (not an individual policy).
2. **Qualified plan** – it must be a health plan that covers hospitalization, routine medical care, and, if possible, prescription drugs.
3. **Tax‑credit eligibility** – for 2024‑2025, the credit is available for premiums for employees aged 18‑64 who are not self‑insured due to the owner’s single‑member LLC status. The credit rate is 50 % for the first year and 25 % for the remaining years under the small‑employer credit rule.  

By choosing a plan that satisfies the “qualified health‑insurance” definition, you gain the dual benefit of providing valuable employee benefits and reducing your tax liability through the available premium deductions and the small‑employer credit.

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11),

---

**STEP 2. Answer**

You must keep business records because they serve several essential purposes:

1. **To manage the business and support financial decisions**  
   Business records show income, expenses, assets, and liabilities.  They help you deal with banks or creditors and manage your operations. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

2. **To identify and separate income sources**  
   Records identify where receipts come from, allowing you to separate business from non‑business income and distinguish taxable from non‑taxable income. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

3. **To record deductible expenses and prevent omissions**  
   When you keep records as expenses occur, you are less likely to forget them when preparing a tax return. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)

4. **To support tax‑return preparation and compliance**  
   Good records are needed to prepare accurate returns and to substantiate the income, deductions, and credits you report. They must be available for IRS inspection and can speed any examination. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

5. **To maintain a reliable recording system**  
   A clear record‑keeping system—whether single‑entry or double‑entry—must show all business transactions, include supporting documents (invoices, receipts, bank records), and be kept daily or monthly. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)

6. **To meet retention requirements**  
   You must keep records for as long as they may be needed for the administration of any provision of the Internal Revenue Code—typically until the applicable period of limitations expires (usually 3–6 years for income‑tax matters, and at least 4 years for employment‑tax matters). [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)

Thus, keeping business records is necessary for sound business management, accurate and defensible tax reporting, compliance with IRS and other regulatory requirements, and for protecting the business in case of audits or disputes.

runs.question: what accounting method should i use
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.  Passages that directly answer the question**

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5),  
[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15),  
[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16),  
[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)

**STEP 2.  Answer**

The IRS lets a business choose its accounting method when it files its first income‑tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040).

- The two basic methods are **cash** and **accrual**.  With a cash method you report income only when you actually receive it and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year you pay them [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  
- With an accrual method you report income in the year it is earned, even if payment comes later, and you deduct or capitalize expenses in the year they are incurred, regardless of when they are paid [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  

**Which method should you use?**

| Consideration | Recommended method |
|---------------|--------------------|
| **No inventory** and the business is a small sole‑proprietor, LLC, or partnership that can keep simple records | **Cash** – it is easier to maintain and works well for businesses that simply track when money comes in and goes out (irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf, page 5; irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf, page 15). |
| **Inventory** is necessary to account for your income | **Accrual** is required for purchases and sales; a small business may keep inventory as a “non‑incidental” item and still use a cash‑style method for other items, but a pure cash method is generally not permitted [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |
| You want to match income and expenses in the same year | **Accrual** provides that match; cash may delay reporting income or expenses until a later year [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15). |
| You need a combination of both for different parts of the business | IRS allows a **combination method** if it “clearly shows your income” and you use it consistently; however, if inventory is involved you must use accrual for that portion [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). |
| You plan to change the method later | After the first return, any change generally requires IRS approval (Form 1128) [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14). |

**Bottom line:**  
If you have no inventory and your bookkeeping is simple, start with the **cash method**.  
If you sell or hold inventory, use the **accrual method** (or a hybrid that applies accrual only to inventory).  
Whichever method you choose, keep the same method each year, use it consistently for all income and expenses, and file the appropriate tax return at that year’s end to adopt the method.

        [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15),  
        [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

**STEP 2. Answer**

Cash and accrual accounting differ in *when* income and expenses are recorded for tax purposes.  

* **Cash method** – income is reported in the year it is actually received, and expenses are generally deducted in the year they are paid (or, if paid in advance, in the year they are applicable) [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

* **Accrual method** – income is reported in the year it is earned, even if the money is received later, and expenses are deducted in the year they are incurred, whether or not they are paid that same year [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5).  

These timing rules also affect how items such as inventory are handled. For example, when you use the accrual method you typically take inventories into account at the beginning and end of the tax year, and you must use an accrual method for purchases and sales of merchandise [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16). In contrast, the cash method usually allows you to deduct expenses when they are actually paid, and it is often used by small, no‑inventory businesses [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15).  


**In short:**  
*Cash = income when received, expenses when paid.*  
*Accrual = income when earned, expenses when incurred.*  

These rules are the core difference between the two accounting methods.

runs.question: can i deduct business travel
runs.answer:
**STEP 1**  


**STEP 2**  
Yes.  The IRS allows a business owner to deduct ordinary and necessary travel expenses that are incurred while traveling away from home for business purposes.  To qualify you must meet two conditions:  

1. Your duties require you to be away from the general area of your tax home (the city or area where your business is located) for a period substantially longer than an ordinary day’s work, and  
2. You need to get sleep or rest to meet the demands of your work while away from home [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  

The deductible travel expenses include:  

- **Transportation** between your home and the business destination (air, train, bus, car) [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
- **Taxi, commuter bus, and limousine fares** between the airport or station and your hotel, or between the hotel and the business location [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
- **Baggage and shipping** costs for sending luggage or sample/display material between your regular and temporary work locations [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).  
- **Vehicle operating and maintenance** costs, including the cost of operating a car or truck when traveling away from home, or the standard mileage rate, plus business‑related tolls and parking [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40).

These expenses must be ordinary (common and accepted in your industry) and necessary (helpful and appropriate for your business) to qualify for the deduction.

runs.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.**  


**STEP 2.**  
If your shop serves the public, you are a **public accommodation** and the ADA obligates you to **remove physical barriers that are “readily achievable.”** This means that, if it can be done without undue difficulty or expense, you must make your shop wheelchair‑accessible [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6).  

If it is not reasonably possible to remove a barrier (for example, because of structural constraints, lack of space, or cost concerns), the ADA allows you to provide **alternative services** such as home delivery or a different accessible location for the same service [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10).  

So, in short, yes—you are required to make your shop wheelchair‑accessible as far as it is readily achievable; otherwise you may offer an alternative means to serve people with disabilities.

runs.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
runs.answer:
**Step 1 – Records that answer the question**  


**Step 2 – Answer**  

**Tax records to keep**  
- Keep all books, receipts, invoices, canceled checks, payroll records, and other documents that support every item of income, deduction, or credit on your tax return until the *period of limitations* for that return expires. The IRS’s Table 3 shows that the limitation period is usually **3 years** for most ordinary returns, 6 years if you fail to report >25 % of income, and *not limited* if you file a fraudulent return [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
- Keep copies of every filed tax return for the same length of time or longer if it is needed to support future returns or amended returns.  
- **Employment‑tax records:** If you have employees, retain all employment‑tax documents for **at least four (4) years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  
- **Asset‑related records:** Maintain records for property (purchase, sale, depreciation, etc.) until the *period of limitations* expires for the year in which you dispose of that property in a taxable transaction. These records are needed to compute depreciation, amortization, or basis for gains/losses [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).

**Injury/illness records to keep**  
- Recordable work‑related injuries and illnesses (excluding minor injuries that require only first aid) must be logged on OSHA Form 300 (Log of Work‑Related Injuries and Illnesses) and supplemented by OSHA Form 301 (Injury and Illness Incident Report) [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
- Keep the OSHA Form 300, 301, and the annual summary Form 300A for **at least five (5) years** at the worksite [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15).  
- If your business falls under the partial exemptions (≤10 workers or certain low‑hazard industries), the same record‑keeping requirements still apply for recordable injuries; only the reporting scope may be reduced.

These passages provide the exact types of records that must be kept and the statutory retention periods required for both tax purposes and OSHA injury/illness reporting.

runs.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
runs.answer:
**STEP 1.  Source passages that actually answer the question**
